text.paragraph: Establishing primary care twelve days after discharge from a first psychiatric admission: provisional diagnosis, antipsychotic monitoring baseline, first-episode workup, alcohol, sleep, and safety planning. Concerns: He wants to understand what happened to him and to stop it happening again, and is frightened that it will; He wants to paint every day again and to be able to concentrate; He is worried about his drinking and his sleep. [S]

Sleep: for several weeks before the episode he slept three or four hours a night while painting, without feeling tired; since discharge about six hours with broken sleep [S]
Meals irregular when he is working, often bread and coffee; drinks several cups of coffee a day [S]
Supports: a friend he paints with who lives nearby, and the coordinated specialty care team; his work is his strongest reason to get well. He decides who is told about his health [S]

tr.td: Continue the antipsychotic started in hospital at the lowest effective dose, with side-effect checks at each visit (akathisia, stiffness, sedation) and monitoring to the APA and ADA/APA standard: weight at every visit, blood pressure, fasting glucose, A1c and lipids at baseline, 12 weeks and yearly, and the AIMS at baseline and every six months
Psychiatry consultation with the first-episode psychosis coordinated specialty care team to review the provisional diagnosis and differential, the dose, the alcohol plan, and the workup for epilepsy

First-episode workup: blood count, metabolic panel, liver tests, thyroid test, vitamin B12, HIV and syphilis tests, urine drug test, brain MRI, and a sleep-deprived EEG because of the confusion and the question of seizures
Alcohol care: AUDIT-C, PEth at each check to follow drinking, brief counseling with goals he chooses, thiamine, and a medicine for alcohol use disorder once the liver tests are reviewed

Coordinated specialty care: a care coordinator, individual resilience-focused therapy, education about psychosis for him and for the people he chooses, support to return to painting and selling his work, and a peer specialist
Sleep as treatment and as an early warning sign: regular sleep and wake times, no alcohol to get to sleep, less coffee after noon, and a plan to call the team after two nights of short sleep
Structured safety assessment, a written safety plan with early warning signs, lethal-means counseling, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, PHQ-9 at each visit, and safety review at every visit
Akathisia: aripiprazole back to 10 mg daily, propranolol 10 mg twice daily for a few weeks, and a check of restlessness and of safety at each visit until it settles
No return of psychotic symptoms and no readmission through six months, on the lowest effective antipsychotic dose
No psychotic symptoms since the six-week visit and no admission; aripiprazole 10 mg daily
PHQ-9 score below 5 by six months
Reduce drinking to PEth below 20 ng/mL by six months

list.item: Independent in all activities; not yet painting since discharge because he cannot concentrate for long; manages his money and medicines [S]

Alert and oriented; quiet and cooperative; speech normal in rate; no current hallucinations by report, though he sometimes hears his name called as he falls asleep; mild suspiciousness at night; thought process organized; insight growing [S]

Mood low and flat, ashamed of the episode, which he cannot remember well; PHQ-9 score 13 with item 9 scored 1 for passive thoughts that it would be easier not to wake up; no intent, plan or preparation; no thoughts of harming others [S]

text.paragraph: Structured synthetic safety assessment on 1889-01-19: current ideation present, intent absent, plan absent. Outpatient care with close follow-up. He has passive thoughts that it would be easier not to wake up, without intent, plan or preparation; the self-injury during the episode happened in confusion and without suicidal intent. His risk is higher in the months after a first episode of psychosis, while he is depressed, and while he is drinking. A written safety plan was made with him, with his own early warning signs (nights with little sleep, hearing voices, drinking more, pulling away from his friend) and what to do about each. Lethal-means counseling: he has no firearm and no access to one and agreed not to acquire one; medicines are dispensed two weeks at a time; he will keep alcohol out of the house while he is low. The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline was given and saved in his phone, with the clinic number. Safety reviewed at every visit [S]
